# How Yammu got its accent back

The ASCII form *yammu* is missing something. **Yammu** restores ​the marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the ‌full scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Phoenician evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. ‌By the end, the marks in Yammu will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** ​Yammu
- **ASCII form:** yammu
- **Meaning:** "Sea"
- **Domain of influence:** Sea, Chaos
- **Pantheon:** Phoenician
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𐤉𐤌 (Phoenician)

## Overview

**Yammu** (*yammu*) — The Sea, Rival of Baʿal · Sea ​— belongs to the Phoenician tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sea, Chaos". The name means "Sea".

**Yammu** is the Canaanite sea-god: the personified ocean whose rebellion against the divine ​council set the Baal Cycle in motion, and whose defeat by Baʿal — with two magic clubs thrown from the storm-cloud — established the storm-god’s kingship over the gods. The Ugaritic ​tablets of the fourteenth century BCE, found in 1929, gave him back his name after three thousand years of silence.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Yammu** and serves its temple at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/yammu/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *yammu* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the ‌restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Phoenician as **𐤉𐤌**. Etymologically it means "Sea".

The ASCII form *yammu* survives ​only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Yammu** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly ​transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **y** → **Y** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** ‌— Same
- **m** → **m** — Same
- **m** → **m** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Phoenician as **𐤉𐤌** — Phoenician alphabet, ​attested Phoenician, c. 1050–800 BCE, in Levant / Mediterranean. The script is written right-to-left.

The scholarly transliteration is *Yammu* (Phoenician linear alphabet), giving the normalized reading /ˈjam.mu/.

The rendering proceeds step by ‌step:

- Phoenician y-m, the Semitic word for 'sea'
- The doubled mm in the absolute state produces Yammu
- Personified Sea in the Baal Cycle

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is ​**/ˈjɑːmʊ/** — Ugaritic (conventional vocalisation).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ym** — Written ym in Ugaritic cuneiform; conventionally vocalised “Yammu”. The word means “sea”.
- **** — The Canaanite sea-god, rival and enemy of Baʿal, ‌defeated in the great Baal Cycle of Ugarit.
- **** — The name needs no vowels the Ugaritic scribes would not have recognised — a plain transliteration.

For the modern speaker, the ​closest approximation is: “YAH-moo”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Akkadian** — Tiamat’s kin — the sea-monster of the Enūma eliš
- **Rival** — Baal (Baʿlu) — the storm-god of the Ugaritic ​tablets

He is the sea itself as god: the oldest named enemy in the Baal Cycle, defeated at the world’s beginning.

## Mythology

Yammu’s mythology is the Baal Cycle’s opening act: the ​sea demands the storm-god’s surrender, the council wavers, and Baʿal — armed by the craftsman-god Kothar-wa-Khasis with two magic clubs — goes out to meet the flood and splits the sea’s skull ​between the eyes. It is the Levant’s own dragon-combat — the same pattern as Marduk and Tiamat, Indra and Vritra, told in the oldest alphabetic literature on earth.

### The Embassy of ​the Sea (KTU 1.2)

The cycle opens with Yammu’s envoys at the divine council, demanding that Baʿal be delivered into the sea’s power. El, the aged king of the gods, wavers — ‌and it is left to Baʿal himself, with Kothar-wa-Khasis’s weapons, to answer the demand. The scene sets the cycle’s whole theology: kingship is taken, not granted.

### The Two Magic Clubs (KTU 1.2 ​iv)

Kothar-wa-Khasis gives Baʿal two clubs — Yaggarish, “Chaser”, and Ayyamarri, “Driver”. Baʿal strikes Yammu between the eyes, on the skull: ‘Yammu is dead! Baʿal is king!’ The lines are the ‌Levantine storm-god’s coronation — and the pattern that Hebrew poetry would echo in its own sea-combat, Yahweh versus Yam.

### Yam in the Psalms (Biblical Echoes)

The Hebrew Bible keeps the sea-god’s name ​as a common noun and his defeat as a motif: ‘Thou didst divide the sea (yam) by thy strength’, ‘thou rulest the raging of the sea (yam)’. The Ugaritic tablets revealed ‌what the Psalms were arguing against — and what they preserved: Yammu’s defeat is the Old Testament sea’s backstory.

### The Sea-Enemy Pattern (Comparative Frame)

Yammu belongs to the oldest myth-complex in the ​lexicon: the storm-god versus the sea. Tiamat and Marduk in Babylon, Vritra and Indra in the Rigveda, Typhon and Zeus in Greece — the pattern crosses the whole ancient world, and ‌the Ugaritic telling is among its most vivid witnesses. The sea is always first, and always beaten.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Yammu concentrates in a small set of recurring ​attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Sea Itself** — His name IS the word “sea” (ym) — the ocean as the first rebel against order.
- **The Two Clubs** ‌— “Chaser” and “Driver”, the magic clubs Baʿal threw to shatter his skull — the cycle’s most quoted scene.
- **The Divine Council** — He demanded Baʿal’s surrender from the council of El; ​the gods’ cowardice set the war in motion.
- **The Tablet’s Return** — Found at Ugarit (Ras Shamra) in 1929 — the Baal Cycle restored Canaanite religion to history.

## Archaeology & Evidence

​The material record for Yammu survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient ‌testimony.

Yammu’s monuments are the tablets: the Baal Cycle’s cuneiform pages from Ras Shamrt (Ugarit), 1929 — the oldest large alphabetic texts ever found, and the foundation-stones of Northwest Semitic philology.

## Across Cultures

Yammu is the Canaanite branch of the ancient Near Eastern ​sea-enemy — Tiamat’s cousin, with the Babylonian goddess-dragon as his nearest kin. The Hebrew tradition suppressed him into a noun but kept his combat; and modern study of the Baal Cycle ​restored him as the indispensable witness to what Israel’s religion argued with. The Greeks of the coast heard Poseidon in him; the scholars hear the pattern.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index include [[angrboda|Angrboða]] (chaos / primordial / world serpent), [[apep|ꜥꜣpp]] (chaos / primordial / world serpent), [[aseratu|Ašeratu]] (sea / water), [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (sea / water), [[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] (sea / water), and [[chaos|Cháos]] (chaos ​/ primordial / world serpent).

## Cultural Legacy

The Baal Cycle’s discovery in 1929 rewrote the history of Canaanite and biblical religion — Yammu’s defeat gave the Psalms their sea-imagery’s original. In Ugaritic ​studies his name heads every syllabus; and the sea-monster pattern he anchors remains the comparative mythologist’s oldest exhibit.

## A Meditation

Yammu: the sea’s own name, restored in plain ‌letters that the fourteenth-century scribes would have recognised. He needs no vowel-marks the tablets did not carry — the plain transliteration IS the restoration, and the skull-split the literature remembers.

## A ‌Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Yammu**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote ​the name in Phoenician rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *yammu* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling ​should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as ​the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **y**, ‌**a**, **m**, **m**, **u** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep ​the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Yammu in Its Tradition

**Yammu** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Phoenician tradition, where it is counted among 7 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. ​Its sphere — Sea, Chaos — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way ​of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Yammu**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living ‌catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, ​between a tradition and a trend. **Yammu** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is ‌a kind of publication. When **Yammu** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index ​it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, ‌a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *yammu*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The ​punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration ‌Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Yammu**, the chain begins with the ‌attested form in Phoenician, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Sea" anchors the name in its semantic field; without ​that anchor, the marks would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Yammu** and the ASCII form *yammu* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a ​conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Yammu aSCII-equivalent form. The ​rule is mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence ​produced it, because every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
